scenario: WIBTA if I refused to translate medical jargon for my family anymore? | I (25f) am a first gen college student, and am almost finished with my nursing degree. My family is all insanely supportive and proud of me, and generously have all come together to cover my expenses as far as rent/food/pocket money/car/insurance etc, so I can be completely focused on school. I’m so increasingly thankful for them all but they’re starting to get on my nerves. Since I’m studying to be a nurse, I can understand and break down medical jargon to my family in a way that they can understand. I never minded, but now it’s starting to get too much because they’ll ask me for medical advice, based on me explaining their jargon. For example, today. My grandfather calls, and asks me to explain to him about Stem Cell Therapy to him. I explain, and then he goes on and asks, “So, should I get stem cells injected into my knees for my bone on bone arthritis?” I try to tell him that I’m not a medical professional, I can’t really prescribe or advise on medical decisions. He started to get upset and basically demanded that I tell him what I thought. I finally broke down and after reiterating four or five times that I’m not a medical professional and told him I wouldn’t advise it, because there’s no evidence that the injections would make his cartilage grow back, but he should mention it to a doctor for a more professional opinion. He decisively tells me that he won’t be doing it, then, because of what I’d said. This is essentially what my whole family does. **I am not a medical professional!** I don’t feel comfortable with my family asking me to ok or veto potential treatments or operations, but they don’t listen when I tell them that though! I feel so guilty because they do so much for me and they expect so little, but I’d hate to give them the wrong advice and cost someone their health or even worse their life. WIBTA if I refused to help out with medical confusion, and instead told them to ask an actual physician?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me to refuse to help my family with their medical questions. I'm a 25-year-old first-gen college student almost done with my nursing degree. My family has been super supportive, covering all my expenses so I can focus on school. I'm really grateful, but lately, they're getting on my nerves a bit. I can understand medical jargon and explain it to them, which I used to be okay with. But now, they're asking me for medical advice based on those explanations. For example, my grandfather asked about stem cell therapy for his arthritis. I tried to explain it and told him I'm not a medical professional, so I can't advise him. He got upset and demanded my opinion. I ended up telling him not to do it because there's no evidence it works, and he should talk to a doctor. He decided not to proceed because of what I said. This happens a lot. My family doesn't listen when I tell them I'm not qualified. I feel guilty because they've done so much for me, but I don't want to give wrong advice that could harm them. I'm considering refusing to help with their medical questions and telling them to ask a real physician instead. Is that the right thing to do? I think about the consequences. If I stop helping, they might be upset, but it's better than giving bad advice. On the other hand, they rely on me because I'm the one with the medical background. Maybe I should set boundaries. I can explain things but make it clear I can't give medical advice. I should encourage them to consult a professional. I also wonder if there's a middle ground. Maybe I can help them understand their options but always stress the importance of talking to a doctor. That way, I'm not giving direct advice but still supporting them. It's a tough balance between being helpful and not overstepping my role. In the end, I think it's better to set clear boundaries. My family's health is too important to risk giving incorrect advice. I'll explain that while I can help them understand medical terms, I can't make decisions for them. They need to consult a licensed physician for proper advice. It might make them upset at first, but it's the responsible thing to do.
